passages.happening:
That same day Jesus goes out and sits by the lake. The crowds are so large that he gets into a boat and sits there to teach, while the people stand on the shore.

He tells them many things in parables, short stories from ordinary life. The first is about a farmer sowing seed. Some falls on the path, and birds eat it. Some falls on rocky ground, springs up quickly, and withers in the sun because it has no root. Some falls among thorns, which choke it. And some falls on good soil and gives a crop, a hundredfold, sixtyfold or thirtyfold. Jesus ends, “He who has ears, let him hear.”
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this parable too (Mark 4:1-9), and the note there explains the farming. A farmer threw seed by hand in wide sweeps as he walked, and some always landed where it could not grow. Scholars still debate whether seed was sown before or after ploughing, and many think farmers did both. Either way, the waste in the story would have sounded normal. The harvest would not. A hundredfold was a mark of God's blessing.

Matthew places this parable at a turning point. Chapters 11 and 12 have shown Jesus refused: by the towns that saw his miracles, by Pharisees who called his work the devil's, even misunderstood by his own family. Now Jesus tells a story about seed that is wasted on bad ground and still brings a great harvest. It explains what the reader has just seen. Many will not receive the message. The harvest will come anyway.

Matthew counts the harvest downward, ‘a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold’, where Mark counts upward. The point is the same. Even the smallest yield of good soil is rich.

This chapter is the third of Matthew's five long blocks of teaching. Like the others, it ends with the words ‘When Jesus had finished’ (verse 53).
passages.ot: The prophets often pictured God's word as seed. Through Isaiah God says that as rain makes the earth give “seed to sow and food to eat,” so His word “will not return to Me empty” (Isaiah 55:10-11). Isaac sowed in a hard land, “and that very year he reaped a hundredfold. And the LORD blessed him” (Genesis 26:12).
passages.asks: The farmer keeps sowing, though much of his seed is lost. Ask whether you have stopped speaking of God, or stopped listening to him, because so much seems wasted. And hear the closing words as a question for you: what kind of ground are you giving him today?

passages.happening:
The disciples come and ask, “Why do You speak to the people in parables?” Jesus answers that the knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven has been given to them, “but not to them.” Whoever has will be given more; whoever does not have will lose even what he has. “This is why I speak to them in parables: ‘Though seeing, they do not see; though hearing, they do not hear or understand.’”

He says this fulfils Isaiah's prophecy, and quotes it in full. Then he turns to the disciples: “But blessed are your eyes because they see, and your ears because they hear.” Many prophets and righteous people longed to see and hear what they are seeing and hearing, and did not.
passages.hearers:
A parable, as the Mark 4 note explains, is a picture laid alongside a truth. It does not explain itself. It leaves the hearer to finish the thought. A ‘mystery’ in the Bible is not a puzzle for clever people. It is a secret of God that he chooses to make known.

Matthew's wording differs from Mark's in one important way. Mark gives Isaiah's words as a purpose: ‘so that’ they may see and not perceive (Mark 4:12). Matthew gives them as a reason: Jesus speaks in parables ‘because’ they already see without seeing (verse 13). After chapters 11 and 12 the reader knows who those people are: the towns that would not turn and the critics who called God's work evil.

Only Matthew quotes the whole of Isaiah's words here. Only Matthew and Luke have the blessing on the disciples' eyes and ears (Luke 10:23-24). The disciples are no smarter than the crowd. In verse 36 they will have to ask what the next parable means. They are blessed because they came and asked.
passages.ot:
The quotation is from Isaiah 6, where God sends Isaiah to a nation that had already turned away. God warns that his preaching will be met with closed ears: “Be ever hearing, but never understanding; be ever seeing, but never perceiving” (Isaiah 6:9).

Compare the next line. In Isaiah, as English Bibles translate the Hebrew, God tells the prophet, “Make the hearts of this people calloused” (Isaiah 6:10). In Matthew the line reads, “this people's heart has grown callous; they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes” (verse 15). In Matthew's form, the people have done it to themselves. And Matthew ends with God's longing: they might “turn, and I would heal them.”
passages.hard:
Does Jesus tell parables so that people will not understand and be healed? On a first reading verses 11 to 15 can sound that way: the knowledge is given to some, ‘but not to them’.

Christians have answered in different ways. John Chrysostom, a preacher of the late 300s, stressed that Jesus says ‘seeing, they do not see’: their blindness was their own choice, and the parables were meant to rouse them, not to shut them out. Many modern readers agree that Matthew's ‘because’ makes the parables a response to hardness already shown, not its cause. Others, in the tradition that stresses God's choosing, hold that Matthew keeps both God's giving (verse 11) and human refusal (verse 15), as Isaiah did, and that the two are not rivals. Christians who stress God's choosing and those who stress human freedom have read these verses differently for centuries. These notes do not settle it.

One misuse should be named. Christians have sometimes read ‘them’ as the Jewish people as a whole. That is wrong. The disciples who are blessed in verse 16 are Jews too, and the warning falls on anyone, in any age, who has ears and will not hear. The chapter keeps the door open with the same call each time: “He who has ears, let him hear.”
passages.asks: The disciples did not understand either. The difference is that they came and asked. Ask whether you treat the hard parts of the Bible as a reason to walk away, or as a reason to come closer. And count what you have been given to see. Prophets longed for it.

passages.happening: Jesus explains the parable of the sower. The seed on the path is the person who hears “the message of the kingdom” but does not understand it, and the evil one snatches it away. The seed on rocky ground is the one who receives the word with joy but has no root; when trouble or persecution comes because of the word, he quickly falls away. The seed among thorns is the one in whom “the worries of this life and the deceitfulness of wealth choke the word.” The seed on good soil is “the one who hears the word and understands it.” He bears fruit.
passages.hearers:
Mark's note on this explanation (Mark 4:13-20) says more about the rocky ground and the thorns. Matthew's first readers, like Mark's, knew what it meant for faith to meet persecution, and what it meant for worry about bread and debt to fill a day.

Matthew's version has one word Mark does not stress: ‘understand’. The seed on the path is the hearer who does not understand (verse 19). The good soil is the hearer who understands (verse 23). In the Bible, to understand is not only to grasp an idea. It is to take the word in so that it shapes a life. That is why the good soil ‘bears fruit’.

‘Falls away’ is the Greek skandalizō, the word for tripping over something. Jesus used it of John in 11:6, and the people of Nazareth will do it at the end of this chapter (13:57).
passages.hard: Did Jesus give this explanation, or did the early church add it? As the Mark 4 note explains, some scholars since Adolf Jülicher in the late 1800s have held that a true parable makes one point, so a point-by-point explanation must be later teaching. Others, such as Craig Blomberg, answer that ancient parables often carried several points and that teachers in Jesus' world sometimes explained their own stories. The Gospels present it as Jesus' own words, and that is how the church has read it.
passages.asks: These are not four kinds of people sorted forever. Most hearts hold some path, some rock, some thorns and some good soil at once. Ask which one is crowding out God's word in you right now. And ask whether you are only hearing, or also understanding: letting the word in far enough to change what you do.

passages.happening:
Jesus tells another parable. A man sows good seed in his field. But while everyone is asleep, an enemy comes, sows weeds among the wheat, and slips away. When the wheat comes up and forms heads, the weeds appear too.

The servants ask the owner, ‘Didn't you sow good seed? Where did the weeds come from?’ “An enemy did this,” he replies. They offer to pull the weeds up. “No,” he says, because they might uproot the wheat with them. “Let both grow together until the harvest.” At harvest time the weeds will be gathered and burned, and the wheat brought into the barn.
passages.hearers:
The weed in the story, the Greek zizanion, is usually identified as darnel, a wild grass. Older translations call it ‘tares’. Its young plants look so like wheat that it is very hard to tell them apart until the heads form. Its grain makes people ill if it is eaten. So the owner's caution is good farming. Pulling the weeds early would rip out wheat by mistake.

Sowing weeds in someone's field was a real kind of spite. Roman law discussed it. A case from the Roman lawyer Ulpian, preserved in the Digest, the great collection of Roman law made in the 500s, deals with a man who sowed weeds in another man's field and spoiled his crop.

This parable is found only in Matthew. Jesus will explain it in verses 36 to 43.
passages.hard:
What is the field, and what should the church do with ‘weeds’? This parable has a long and painful history.

In North Africa in Augustine's day, around AD 400, a church called the Donatists claimed to be the pure church, made up only of the faithful. They pointed out that Jesus says “The field is the world” (verse 38), not the church, so the church itself must be kept pure now. Augustine of Hippo answered that the church spread through the world is itself a mixed field, with wheat and weeds growing side by side until the harvest. The argument came to a head at a great conference in Carthage in 411. Yet the same parable was later used to justify violence. Thomas Aquinas, in the 1200s, argued that the command not to pull the weeds applies only when the wheat would be harmed, and so heretics could rightly be put to death. Others read it the opposite way. In 1644 Roger Williams, the founder of Rhode Island, argued in The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution that because the field is the world, rulers must leave dissenters and unbelievers alone until God's harvest. John Cotton answered him that the field was the church.

Christians still differ on how this parable bears on church discipline. Some read it as about the world, and leave the church's own discipline to Jesus' words in 18:15-17. Others, following Augustine, read it as calling the church to great patience with its own mixed membership. These notes do not choose between them.

What the story itself says is plain. The servants are told not to pull up the weeds. Judgment belongs to the owner at the harvest. Whatever else this parable teaches, it gives no one a warrant to harm the people they judge to be weeds.
passages.asks: The servants were eager to tidy the field, and the owner told them to wait. Ask where you are quick to sort people into wheat and weeds, in your church, your family, or your politics. Leaving the final judgment to God is not the same as not caring. It is trusting that he sees what you cannot.

passages.t: The mustard seed and the leaven
passages.happening:
Jesus tells two short parables. The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed a man planted in his field. It is the smallest of seeds, but it grows into the largest of garden plants and becomes a tree, so the birds come and nest in its branches.

The kingdom of heaven is also like leaven that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour, until all of it was leavened.

Matthew adds that Jesus told the crowds nothing without a parable. This fulfilled the prophet's words: “I will open My mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world.”
passages.hearers:
The mustard seed is in Mark too (Mark 4:30-32), and the note there explains it. The plant was most likely black mustard, which grows wild in Galilee. Its seed is a millimetre or two across, and in one season the plant can grow two or three metres high. The seed was a byword for the tiniest amount. Mark calls it the largest of garden plants. Matthew and Luke add that it ‘becomes a tree’ (Luke 13:19).

Leaven was a lump of old, fermented dough kept back from the last baking and worked into the new batch to make it rise. A little leaven spread through everything. In the Bible leaven is often a picture of something bad spreading. Jesus will warn, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees” (16:6). Here it is a picture of good. The kingdom works its way through the whole world from the inside.

Three measures of flour was a large batch. It was the amount Sarah used to bake for her three heavenly visitors. Matthew's Greek says the woman ‘hid’ the leaven in the flour, the same family of word as ‘hidden’ in verse 35 and verse 44. The kingdom is hidden now, and it is everywhere at work.
passages.ot:
The birds in the branches recall the prophets' pictures of great kingdoms. In Ezekiel God plants a cedar, and “Birds of every kind will nest under it” (Ezekiel 17:23). In Daniel a great tree stands for a mighty king, and “in its branches the birds of the air nested” (Daniel 4:12). Jesus attaches that picture to a garden plant.

Sarah's baking is in Genesis 18:6, where Abraham tells her to prepare “three seahs of fine flour.”

The quotation in verse 35 is from Psalm 78:2: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the beginning.” Psalm 78 is headed “A Maskil of Asaph,” and Asaph is called “Asaph the seer” in 2 Chronicles 29:30, which may be why Matthew calls him ‘the prophet’. The psalm goes on to tell Israel's history as a lesson. Matthew sees Jesus' parables bringing out what God had kept hidden.
passages.hard: Is the mustard seed really ‘the smallest of all seeds’? Botanists know smaller ones, such as orchid seeds. As the Mark 4 note says, Jesus is speaking as a farmer would, of seeds sown in a field or garden. Among those, mustard was the smallest anyone handled, and it was the common saying for something tiny. Christians who hold that the Bible is without error in every detail, and those who hold it is without error in what it means to teach, both read the line as the speech of the field, not a botany textbook.
passages.asks: God often starts small and works out of sight: a seed in a garden, a lump of dough in a bowl. Ask where you have written something off because it looked too small or too slow, in the church, in your home, or in your own faith. And ask where God might be working in you now, hidden, like leaven.

passages.happening:
Jesus leaves the crowds and goes into the house. His disciples ask him to explain the parable of the weeds.

He tells them: the sower of good seed is the Son of Man. “The field is the world.” The good seed are the sons of the kingdom, and the weeds are the sons of the evil one, sown by the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the harvesters are angels. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will weed out of his kingdom every cause of sin and all who practise lawlessness, and throw them into the fiery furnace, “where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” Then the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom. “He who has ears, let him hear.”
passages.hearers:
The disciples had to ask. Understanding came to them the same way it comes to anyone: by coming close and asking.

‘The end of the age’ is a phrase only Matthew uses in the Gospels. It means the close of this present time, when God puts all things right. Matthew's Gospel ends with Jesus' promise to be with his disciples ‘to the very end of the age’ (28:20).

‘Weeping and gnashing of teeth’ is one of Matthew's own phrases. He uses it six times; Luke once. It is a picture of grief and bitter regret. Matthew used it already of ‘the sons of the kingdom’ who are shut out (8:12), which is a warning to those who think they are safely inside.

The harvesters are angels, not the servants. In the story the servants are not trusted with the sorting, and in the explanation people are not either.
passages.ot:
The fiery furnace recalls the furnace in Daniel, into which those who would not bow to the king's statue were to be thrown (Daniel 3:6). In Malachi, “the day is coming, burning like a furnace, when all the arrogant and every evildoer will be stubble” (Malachi 4:1).

The righteous who ‘shine like the sun’ echo Daniel's promise for the end: “the wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens, and those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever” (Daniel 12:3).
passages.hard:
What is the ‘fiery furnace’, and what is hell like? Christians agree that Jesus warned of real and final judgment. They differ on its nature. The view most widely held through church history is that it is endless, conscious separation from God. Others hold that the wicked will finally cease to exist. Still others hope that God's love will in the end restore all people. Christians also differ on how far the fire and the darkness (8:12) are literal, since the Bible uses both pictures for the same reality. These notes state the views and do not settle the question.

The warning is not meant to frighten anyone into faith, and it is not the whole picture. The same Jesus who warns is the one who says, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (11:28). If you are afraid of God's judgment, hear that voice first. Notice too who is gathered out: ‘every cause of sin and all who practice lawlessness’. The parable does not tell us to look at our neighbours and decide which ones are weeds. It tells us that God will finish the work, justly, and that the righteous will shine.
passages.asks: Evil in the world is real, and it was sown by an enemy, not by God. Ask whether you have blamed God for weeds he did not plant. And ask where you are rooted. The harvest is coming. Are you growing toward the light, so that on that day you will shine?

passages.t: The hidden treasure and the pearl
passages.happening:
Two short parables. The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field. When a man found it, he hid it again, and “in his joy he went and sold all he had and bought that field.”

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant looking for fine pearls. When he found one very precious pearl, he went away and sold all he had and bought it.
passages.hearers:
Buried treasure was not a fairy tale. There were no banks for ordinary people, and armies passed through often. Families hid coins and valuables in the ground, and if the owner died or fled, the hoard could lie forgotten. The historian Josephus says that after Jerusalem fell in AD 70, the Romans dug up much of the gold, silver and other valuables the Jews had buried against the dangers of war, and captives showed them where to find more. A day labourer ploughing someone else's field might strike a jar of coins.

Pearls were among the costliest things in the ancient world. Pliny the Elder, a Roman writer of the 70s AD, said pearls held the very first rank among all valuable things. The merchant here, the Greek emporos, is a wholesale trader who travels to buy, not a village shopkeeper. Matthew also has Jesus warn against throwing ‘pearls before swine’ (7:6).

The two men are different. One stumbles on his treasure by accident. The other spends his life searching. Both, once they find it, sell everything.
passages.ot: Proverbs uses the same pictures for wisdom. Seek it “like silver and search it out like hidden treasure” (Proverbs 2:4). Wisdom “is more precious than rubies; nothing you desire compares with her” (Proverbs 3:15).
passages.hard:
Was the man in the field honest to hide the treasure and buy the field without telling the owner? Jesus does not say, and the parable does not turn on it. Jesus sometimes uses people who are not models of good behaviour to make a point, as in Luke's story of the shrewd manager (Luke 16:1-8). The point here is the joy and the cost: nothing else is worth keeping next to this.

Who is the buyer? Most readers take him as the person who finds the kingdom and gives up everything for it. Others read the buyer as Christ, who gave everything to win his people, with the treasure or the pearl standing for them. Both readings are held. Each says something true about the kingdom: it is worth everything to us, and we were worth everything to him.
passages.asks: Notice the words ‘in his joy’. He did not sell everything grimly, as a sacrifice. He sold it gladly, because he had found something better. Ask whether following Jesus feels to you more like a loss or like a find. What are you holding on to that you would let go of gladly, if you saw what he is worth?

passages.t: The net, and the scribe with new and old
passages.happening:
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea that catches all kinds of fish. When it is full, the fishermen pull it ashore, sit down, and sort the good fish into baskets and throw the bad away. So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will separate the wicked from the righteous.

Jesus asks, “Have you understood all these things?” They answer, “Yes.” Then he says, “For this reason, every scribe who has been discipled in the kingdom of heaven is like a homeowner who brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old.”
passages.hearers:
Several of the disciples were fishermen from this lake, so this picture was their own work. The net here, the Greek sagēnē, was a dragnet: a long net weighted at the bottom and drawn through the water, catching everything in its path. Sorting the catch on the shore was part of every day's work. Under the Law, any water creature without fins and scales was unclean and could not be eaten (Leviticus 11:9-10), so some of the catch was always thrown away.

A ‘scribe’ was a trained teacher of the Scriptures. Matthew has shown many scribes opposing Jesus. Here Jesus speaks of a different kind: one ‘discipled in the kingdom’. The Greek verb is mathēteuō, ‘to make a disciple’, the same word Jesus uses at the end of the Gospel: “make disciples of all nations” (28:19).

The ‘new and old’ treasures are the teaching of Jesus and the Scriptures of Israel, held together. Many readers think this is a picture of what Matthew's own Gospel does, bringing out the old promises and showing them fulfilled in Jesus.
passages.ot:
The prophets used the fishing net as a picture of God's people being gathered, or of judgment. Habakkuk complains of a foe who “catches them in his dragnet” (Habakkuk 1:15). Through Jeremiah God says, “I will send for many fishermen, declares the LORD, and they will catch them” (Jeremiah 16:16).

Jesus has already said, “I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them” (5:17). The scribe of the kingdom does not throw away the old to make room for the new. He brings out both.
passages.asks: The net catches everything, and the sorting is not done by the fishermen in the boat but at the end, on the shore. Ask whether you are trying to do the sorting now. Then think about the storeroom. Are you bringing out only the old, or only the new? A disciple needs both the Scriptures and Jesus who fulfils them.

passages.happening:
When Jesus has finished these parables, he leaves and comes to his home town. He teaches in the synagogue, and the people are astonished. “Where did this man get such wisdom and miraculous powers?” they ask. “Isn't this the carpenter's son? Isn't His mother's name Mary, and aren't His brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas? Aren't all His sisters with us as well?”

“And they took offense at Him.” Jesus says, “Only in his hometown and in his own household is a prophet without honor.” And he did not do many miracles there, because of their unbelief.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this scene too (Mark 6:1-6), and the note there explains it. Nazareth was a small farming village in the hills of Galilee. Most estimates are a few hundred people. Everyone knew everyone, and they had watched Jesus grow up. The word for carpenter, tektōn, means a builder or craftsman, usually in wood. A village builder was a respected working man, but not a rabbi.

Matthew tells it a little differently. Mark has the people say ‘Isn't this the carpenter?’; Matthew has ‘the carpenter's son’. Mark says Jesus ‘could not’ do miracles there; Matthew says he ‘did not do many’. The words ‘took offense’ are the Greek skandalizō, the same as in Jesus' blessing to John: happy is the one who does not ‘fall away on account of Me’ (11:6). Nazareth tripped over Jesus because he was too familiar.

The chapter ends where the parables began. The seed fell on hard ground, and here is the hard ground: his own town.
passages.hard:
Who were Jesus' brothers and sisters? Matthew names four brothers and mentions sisters. Christians have understood them in three ways: as later children of Mary and Joseph (the common Protestant view), as Joseph's children by an earlier marriage (the Orthodox view), or as cousins (a long Catholic view).

Each reading has its texts. The first points to Matthew 1:25, that Joseph “had no union with her until she gave birth to a Son,” and to Luke calling Jesus her “firstborn” (Luke 2:7). The other two point out that the Bible uses ‘brother’ for wider family, as when Abram calls his nephew Lot a brother (Genesis 13:8). They note that Matthew later names “Mary the mother of James and Joseph” at the cross (27:56), apparently not Jesus' mother, and that Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple (John 19:26-27). For Catholic and Orthodox Christians, Mary's lifelong virginity is settled teaching. All three views confess what Matthew 1 teaches plainly: that Jesus was born of the virgin Mary. The question is one on which faithful Christians differ, and these notes do not settle it.

The story did not end at Nazareth. John says “even His own brothers did not believe in Him” (John 7:5). But after the resurrection his brothers were praying with the disciples (Acts 1:14), and the risen Jesus “appeared to James” (1 Corinthians 15:7).
passages.asks: The people of Nazareth thought they already knew all there was to know about Jesus. Ask whether you have grown so used to him, perhaps from childhood, that you no longer expect him to surprise you. And if your own family does not yet believe, remember his brothers. Unbelief at home was not the end of their story.
